get.summary: Liveness probe. Public, and says nothing but whether the service is up.

200.description: The service is up.

get.summary: This contract, served by the running application.

200.description: The OpenAPI document.

post.summary: Sign in with an email and a password; answers with a bearer token and the account's public fields.

200.description: Signed in. Body: { token, user: { id, role, name } }.

401.description: Wrong password, unknown address, or a soft-deleted account — the body does not distinguish them.

422.description: Well-formed JSON, but the credentials were the wrong shape. The body names the fields and never their values.

429.description: Too many failed sign-ins for this account or from this network address. The body does not say which, because which one it was would say whether the account exists.

get.summary: Whoever the bearer token resolves to. Guarded.

200.description: Body: { id, role, name }.

401.description: No token, or one that is malformed, tampered with, expired, foreign-signed, or issued to an account since removed.

post.summary: Change your own password, knowing the current one. One route for every role: an admin doing this uses it too, which is why the admin route for setting somebody else's password refuses a caller their own account — an admin who could skip the current-password check on themselves would turn a stolen session into a permanent one. Body: { currentPassword, newPassword }. Tokens issued before the change stay valid until they expire; ending them is IDENTITY-8-API, and that is a stated gap.

200.description: { id, updatedAt }. No password and no hash, here or in the audit row.

401.description: The current password is wrong. Sign-in gives one refusal for three causes so the response cannot be used to learn which addresses exist; that reasoning does not reach here, because this caller is already authenticated and already knows the account exists. Telling them which half they got wrong leaks nothing.

422.description: `fields` names it: `currentPassword` when it is missing, `newPassword` when it is missing, below the twelve-character floor, or equal to the current one — a change that changes nothing is a change somebody believes they made.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

get.summary: A customer's own tickets. Deliberately not GET /tickets with a different answer for a different caller: the queue belongs to the desk (SC-1) and refuses a customer, and a route whose meaning depended on who asked would make "what does GET /tickets return" a question with two answers. The customer is taken from the subject and never from a parameter. Paginated, filterable and ordered by exactly the code the desk's queue uses.

200.description: A page of tickets: { items, total, limit, offset }, the same envelope every list here answers with.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: Staff asking. They have the queue; answering this for them would be a second way to ask one question, with a subject that has no customer behind it.

422.description: A filter or a page window the rules refuse; `fields` names it.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

post.summary: Create a staff account. Answers with the account and, once, the password it was given.

201.description: Created. Body: { user, initialPassword } — the password is shown here and never again.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: The subject is not an admin. The service is never entered.

409.description: The address already belongs to an account, live or disabled.

422.description: The body was the wrong shape. It names the fields and never their values.

200.description: Body: { items, total, limit, offset }.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: The subject is not an admin. The service is never entered.

422.description: A limit above the ceiling, or a malformed window. Refused, not clamped.

200.description: Body: { user, changed }. changed is false when the role was already that.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: The subject is not an admin. The service is never entered.

404.description: No live account with that id.

409.description: It would leave the system with no administrator.

422.description: The role is not one this system has.

post.summary: Disable an account. Nothing is deleted; the row keeps its history.

200.description: Body: { user }, with deletedAt set.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: The subject is not an admin. The service is never entered.

409.description: Already disabled, or it would leave the system with no administrator.

post.summary: Re-enable a disabled account. It is the same row it always was.

200.description: Body: { user }, with deletedAt cleared.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: The subject is not an admin. The service is never entered.

409.description: Already live, or the address was taken by a live account while this one was disabled.

post.summary: An admin sets another user's password, so somebody locked out gets back in. There is no reset by email in this product — the brief puts it under "Specified only" — which is why a person who forgets theirs needs a colleague rather than a link. The body is { password }; twelve characters is the floor and there are no composition rules, because a rule demanding a symbol produces the same password with a symbol on the end. Nothing comes back but the id and the time: the admin typed it, so there is nothing to read. Tokens issued before this stay valid until they expire — ending them is IDENTITY-8-API, and that is a stated gap rather than an oversight.

200.description: { id, updatedAt }. No password and no hash, here or in the audit row.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: Not an admin — or an admin naming themselves. Setting somebody else's password is for a person who is locked out; changing your own is IDENTITY-7-API and asks for the current one, and an admin who could skip that check on themselves would turn a stolen session into a permanent one.

409.description: The account is disabled. Bringing somebody back is re-enable, with its own route and its own audit row; setting a password through this door would leave the account's state saying one thing and its access saying another.

422.description: The password is missing or shorter than the floor; `fields` names it.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

get.summary: The live staff a ticket can be assigned to. Any signed-in staff member may read it — an agent who cannot see the list cannot hand a ticket over.

200.description: { items, total, limit, offset }. Each item is { id, name, role } — no address, no timestamps, nothing about the password.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

422.description: A limit above the ceiling, or a malformed window. Refused, never clamped (BR-4).

get.summary: Find customers by name, email address or phone number, or list them when no term is given. Any signed-in staff member may read it — an agent who cannot find a customer cannot answer the phone.

200.description: { items, total, limit, offset }. Each item is { id, name, email, phone, createdAt, updatedAt }. A term that matches nothing is an empty page with a total of zero, never a 404.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

422.description: A limit above the ceiling, or a malformed window. Refused, never clamped (BR-4).

post.summary: Put a customer on file, typically while somebody is still on the telephone. A name is required and nothing else is: somebody who telephones may have neither an address nor a number worth keeping, and the desk still needs them. A blank email or phone is the same as none — both are stored as absent, so "one live customer per address" keeps its meaning. Writes a customers row and no users row: the two are separate tables (I-1), and a customer gets a sign-in through a different story.

201.description: The customer that was created, with the id the caller needs next.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

422.description: A missing name, an email that is not one, or an address already held by a live customer. The body names the fields, never their values. A retired customer does not hold their address against a new one — the unique index is partial and this refusal asks the same question it does.

get.summary: One customer, whole: their details, the tickets the desk still owes them something on, and their notes — in one answer, read inside one transaction. A screen that assembled this from three requests would be showing three different moments as if they were one. "Open" here means every status the desk has not finished with (new, open, pending, reopened), which is not the same as the status called open. A retired customer still reads back: the list hides them, reading a known id does not, and their tickets did not stop existing. Nothing is audited — a read is not a mutation.

200.description: { customer, tickets: { items, total, limit, offset }, notes: { items, total } }. The tickets are paginated with the ceiling every list obeys; the notes come back whole up to that same ceiling and carry their total, so more than a page of them is visible rather than silently dropped.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such customer. A customer with nothing on file is a 200 with empty lists — that is a different answer.

422.description: A limit above the ceiling, or a malformed window. Refused, never clamped (BR-4).

get.summary: The internal notes about a customer, oldest first. Any signed-in staff member may read them.

200.description: { items, total, limit, offset }. Each item is { id, customerId, authorId, body, createdAt }. authorId is null when the system wrote the note. The order is the order they were written.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such customer, or one that has been removed. Its notes are not readable.

422.description: A limit above the ceiling, or a malformed window. Refused, never clamped (BR-4).

post.summary: Write an internal note about a customer. Audited in the same transaction as the write, so neither can exist without the other.

201.description: The note: { id, customerId, authorId, body, createdAt }.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such customer, or one that has been removed. Nothing is written.

422.description: An absent or blank note. The body names the field, never the value.

post.summary: Raise a ticket for a customer. Any signed-in staff member may; there is one queue and nothing to route it to. The ticket is created, its two service-level clocks are started and an audit row is written in one transaction. Every ticket carries allowedTransitions: the statuses it may legally move to from where it is, derived from the same table a refusal reads. A screen offers those and no others — the 409 is the backstop, not the interface.

201.description: The ticket: { id, customerId, categoryId, assigneeId, status, priority, subject, body, revision, createdAt, updatedAt }. status is always new; priority defaults to normal when none is stated; revision is 1 and is the token a later write sends back (BR-5).

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such customer, or one that has been removed. Nothing is written.

422.description: A missing subject or body, or a stated priority that is not one of low, normal, high, urgent. The body names the fields, never their values. A categoryId that does not exist, or one that has been retired, is refused here too — a retired category satisfies the foreign key and is still not a choice, so the service checks what the constraint cannot see.

get.summary: The queue. Every signed-in staff member sees every ticket in it — there is one organisation and one queue, so it is not scoped to the caller. Filters combine; assigneeId=none means unassigned; the only sort is created_at, newest first, and an unknown one is refused rather than ignored. Every ticket carries allowedTransitions: the statuses it may legally move to from where it is, derived from the same table a refusal reads. A screen offers those and no others — the 409 is the backstop, not the interface.

200.description: { items, total, limit, offset }. Each item is the ticket shape POST returns, including revision — a caller that later writes sends that value back (BR-5). total counts the matches, not the page.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

422.description: A status, priority or sort the API does not name, an empty assigneeId or categoryId, or a limit above the ceiling. The body names the parameters, never their values.

get.summary: The categories a form offers when raising a ticket. Read-only: the seed is where categories are defined and no screen edits them. A retired category leaves this list, but a ticket that already carries one still reads it back — the list and the ticket answer two different questions. Paginated, filterable by q on the name, sortable by name (the default) or created_at, with the page ceiling every list obeys (BR-4).

200.description: { items, total, limit, offset }. Each item is { id, name, createdAt, updatedAt }. Reading writes no audit row.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

422.description: A limit above the ceiling, a sort this list does not know, or a q longer than the ceiling. Refused, never clamped (BR-4). The body names the fields, never their values.

post.summary: Add a category, without a migration and without touching the seed. SC-3 says the seed produces a working system; it does not say the system is stuck with what the seed produced. Admin only. One live category per name, case-insensitively — the column is COLLATE NOCASE and two categories differing only in case are one category typed twice, in a picker whose reports would then not add up. The name is checked before the unique index can fire, because an index that fires gives a raw SQLite error and a 500 that tells an admin their reasonable request was our fault.

201.description: The category: { id, name, createdAt, updatedAt }.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: Not an admin. Reading the list is any staff member’s; managing it is not.

422.description: The name is missing, blank, too long, or already a live category’s; `fields` names it.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

patch.summary: Rename a category. Every ticket already carrying it reads back with the new name, because a ticket references the category rather than copying its name — which is what makes a rename possible at all. A retired category is not renamed: its name is what the tickets carrying it say happened, and BR-1 keeps them for exactly that. Renaming a category to what it is already called is accepted, because refusing it would make "no change" indistinguishable from "that name is taken".

200.description: The category, renamed.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No live category with that id — including one that has been retired.

422.description: The name is missing, blank, too long, or another live category’s; `fields` names it.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

delete.summary: Retire a category. Soft, like every removal here (BR-1): it leaves the list the ticket form offers and stops being choosable for new tickets, and the tickets already carrying it keep it and still read back — a category that vanished from its tickets would rewrite history to tidy a picker. Its name goes back on the shelf, because the unique index is scoped to live rows.

200.description: { id, retiredAt }.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No live category with that id — including one already retired.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

patch.summary: Assign a ticket, or return it to nobody by sending assigneeId null. The caller sends the revision it read; a mismatch is refused rather than overwriting somebody else's change (BR-5). The assignment is audited with both the previous assignee and the new one.

200.description: The ticket, with its new assigneeId and its revision one higher. That new revision is what the next write on this ticket must send.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such ticket, or one that has been removed.

409.description: The revision sent is not the ticket's current one — somebody changed it since it was read. Nothing is written, and re-reading the ticket gives the revision to retry with.

422.description: A missing or malformed revision, or an assigneeId that is not live staff. The body names the fields, never their values.

patch.summary: Move a ticket to another status. The legal moves are a table, not a chain of checks, so a refusal can name what would have worked (T-7). new to resolved is legal: a request answered on the spot should not have to be opened first. closed is the end of the line — reopening lives inside a 14-day window that has passed by the time a ticket is closed. Resolving also requires a note, and it is stored trimmed and readable afterwards — a requirement to write something that is then discarded is theatre. No other move asks for one, and a note sent on another move is ignored rather than stored. The note survives reopening and closing. The caller sends the revision it read (BR-5), and the move is audited with the status before and after.

200.description: The ticket at its new status, with its revision one higher. That new revision is what the next write on this ticket must send.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such ticket, or one that has been removed. A customer gets this for somebody else's ticket, and for any move on their own except reopening it: resolving, closing and pending are the desk saying something about work it is doing.

409.description: One of three, told apart by the code. ILLEGAL_TRANSITION: the move is not in the table, and `allowed` lists the statuses that were legal from where the ticket is — an empty array when the ticket is closed, which is an answer and not a missing field. STATUS_UNCHANGED: the ticket already has that status, and `allowed` is present for the same reason. REVISION_MISMATCH: the move was legal but the revision was stale; `allowed` is absent, because nothing else the caller could have asked for would have worked either. Nothing is written in any of the three. REOPEN_WINDOW_CLOSED is the third 409 here: a resolved ticket may be reopened for fourteen days (T-5) and this one is older. The move is legal and the moment is not, which is why it is not ILLEGAL_TRANSITION. The window is measured from when the ticket was resolved, not from when it was last touched, and it applies to whoever is asking — T-6 closes a resolved ticket after the same fourteen days, so afterwards there is nothing to reopen.

422.description: A status outside the six, a missing or malformed revision, or a resolve with no note — a note that is only whitespace is no note. The body names the fields, never their values. This is 422 and not 409 on purpose: resolving is a legal move, so a missing note is a malformed request and not an illegal transition.

patch.summary: Change a ticket's category. The third write that carries BR-5's revision: the revision the caller read goes in the WHERE, and a mismatch is 409 rather than an overwrite of something they did not see. `null` is a real value meaning no category — the column allows it and a ticket may legitimately have none. A retired category is refused naming the field, checked here rather than left to the foreign key, which can see that a row exists and cannot see that it was taken off the list: what may not be chosen for a new ticket may not be chosen for an old one.

200.description: The ticket, with its new category and its bumped revision.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such ticket — and the same answer a customer gets, because a ticket's filing is the desk's.

409.description: REVISION_MISMATCH: somebody changed the ticket between the read and this write.

422.description: The revision is missing or not a positive integer, or the category is absent, malformed, or one that has been retired; `fields` names it.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

get.summary: Everything that has happened to one ticket, oldest first. Each entry says who, what changed, and from what to what — an entry recording only the new value cannot answer "who took it off me". The order does not depend on two changes having different timestamps: the clock is whole seconds, so two moves inside one second share a time and insertion order breaks the tie. The stored JSON column is parsed here rather than handed over, because a client parsing the storage format makes the storage format the contract. Reading a trail is not an event on it, so nothing is audited.

200.description: { items, total, limit, offset }. Each item is { id, actorId, verb, at, before, after }; actorId is null where the system acted, never invented. A ticket with no history yet is an empty page, not an error.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such ticket. A missing ticket and an empty history are different answers, and only one is an error.

422.description: A limit above the ceiling, or a malformed window. Refused, never clamped (BR-4).

post.summary: An agent replies, in public. The first public reply on a `new` ticket moves it to `open` (T-2) and stops the first-response clock at the reply's own timestamp — once, in the sense that a second reply finds the clock already stopped and the status already moved and changes neither. Nothing counts replies. An internal note stops no clock and moves no status; it has its own story. The reply, its audit row, the clock stop and the status move commit in one transaction, so a ticket cannot end up answered without saying so.

201.description: The message: { id, ticketId, authorId, kind, body, createdAt }. kind is always `public` here — the caller does not choose it.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

403.description: A customer asking. Replying on your own ticket is CONVERSATION-3-API, and it is a different rule with a different effect.

404.description: No such ticket — the same answer every route under a ticket gives.

422.description: The body is missing, blank, or longer than a ticket body may be; `fields` names it.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

get.summary: A ticket's thread, for whoever is reading it. A customer sees the public replies and no sign that anything else exists — not a redaction, not a gap, and not a total that counts what they cannot read: a total including the notes would tell them how many there are, which is the leak wearing a number. Staff see both kinds and each row says which it is, because an agent about to write something they would not say to a customer needs to know which they are looking at. The filter is in the query rather than applied to the rows afterwards, so the notes are never fetched for a reader who may not have them. Oldest first, paginated like every list here.

200.description: { items, total, limit, offset }. Each message is { id, ticketId, authorId, kind, body, createdAt }; for a customer every kind is `public`.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No such ticket — and the same answer, byte for byte, for a customer asking about somebody else's.

422.description: A page window the rules refuse; `fields` names it.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

post.summary: The public intake. A stranger with no token submits a request and it becomes a ticket — raised through the same service the desk uses, so the same validation, the same service-level clocks and the same audit row apply. This is the only unauthenticated route besides sign-in, and deliberately so: SC-2 says every rule is enforced in the API, and a second write path would be a second set of rules that agree until they do not. The customer is resolved from the email address, or created then and there if nobody has it (I-2, I-4); nobody is signed in, so both audit rows name the system as their actor. The channel is a path segment and is recorded on the ticket.

201.description: The ticket, exactly as a desk-raised one reads: { id, customerId, categoryId, assigneeId, status, priority, subject, body, revision, resolutionNote, allowedTransitions, channel, createdAt, updatedAt }. status is new and assigneeId is null — arriving from outside is not a priority.

404.description: No channel by that name — one nothing here has ever heard of. A channel this system knows about and has decided against answers 501 instead.

501.description: Named, and deliberately not built. The channel is one this system knows about — email, whatsapp and sms are under "Specified only" in the product brief — and has decided against. The body carries `name`, the channel it is about, beside the shared { code, requestId }: a bare code would say it is not built and not what is not built. Distinct from 404 on purpose (E-3): 404 says there is no such thing, which about a channel somebody considered and rejected would hide the decision rather than state it.

422.description: The ticket's own fields are malformed: fields names them. Checked before the customer is resolved, so a refused request leaves no customer behind. A missing or malformed email address is refused here too, naming email.

429.description: Too many requests from this address. The intake counts every arrival — successes as well as refusals — because a flood of well-formed submissions is exactly the shape a public form is attacked with, and a counter that only counted failures could be walked straight past. Sixty per address per minute; the window is anchored to the first arrival in it and reopens on its own. The address is the socket peer: no proxy trust is configured, so behind a reverse proxy this would be the proxy.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.

post.summary: Give a customer a way in. Creates a `users` row with role `customer` and points `customers.user_id` at it — the link rule I-1 describes, written. One transaction: an account with no link belongs to nobody, and a link with no account points at nothing. The role carries no permission an agent has; a customer reads their own ticket's history and every other route refuses them. Any signed-in staff member may, because the agent is the one on the phone.

201.description: { customer, user, initialPassword }. The password travels once, here, and nothing reads it back — the same contract creating a staff account has. The agent reads it out.

401.description: No token, or one that does not resolve to a live account.

404.description: No live customer with that id. A removed customer is kept for the trail, not for writing to (BR-1).

409.description: That customer already has a sign-in. Checked here rather than left to the partial unique index on user_id, because an index that fires produces a raw SQLite error and a 500 — which tells the caller their reasonable question was our fault.

422.description: The customer has no email address, and `fields` names it. The address is what they would sign in with (I-4); inventing one for them would be inventing an identity.

500.description: Unhandled, logged with the request id.
